newsitem.title: USA: CMS says Atacama could be over $1.0 billion.
newsitem.headline: CMS says Atacama could be over $1.0 billion.

text.p: CMS Energy Corp believes that its Atacama pipeline-power project could eventually amount to over $1.0 billion, company president Victor Fryling told Reuters in a telephone interview.

CMS and Empresa Nacional de Electricidad S.A. on Thursday placed contracts worth $650 million for 925 kilometres of pipeline and 710 megawatts of generating plant for their electricity project in the Chilean mining region.
Desalinisation facilities alone would add $80-$100 million to the cost of the project, Fryling said.
CMS has an ambitious plan to generate some 35-40 percent of its operating revenues overseas by the year 2001 from 19 percent now.
The company has four power plants in Argentina and a distribution as well as energy extraction facilities and has oil and gas drilling operations in Colombia and Ecuador, which it may expand.
"Colombia is a very attractive market because it is a resource-rich country and while Ecuador is primarily oil we have been looking at power production there," Fryling said.

The company recently bought a 420 kilometre gas pipeline in Western Australia and offshore gasfields for some $120 million and plans to participate in what Fryling described as the $2.0 billion privatisation opportunities which are still to come in the region.
The company plans to build gas storage at a cost of $50-$60 at its existing Western Australia operations.
CMS was also part of the consortium which bought the 2,000 megawatt Loy Yang power station in Australia for A$4.8 billion.
The company also has a couple of greenfield billion dollar deals on the initial stages on the drawing board.
"We have a few projects in the Indonesian and Asian market which could be north of a billion dollars but none are at the point where could attach a high degree of certainty of getting them done.

Asked whether increased competition in the developing world meant that returns on projects would decline, Fryling said that much of the competition was using the international arena as a temporary shelter from the regulatory chaos of the U.S. market.
"These companies are using it as a five year strategy, we are more interested outside the U.S. than inside," he said. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
